result:
**Short version:** I fixed 15 violations: 8 of Rule 1 (figurative or uncommon wording), 1 of Rule 2, 5 of Rule 3 (long or nested sentences) and 1 of Rule 4. Rule 8 (undefined terms) is not fixed, because the passages are excerpts and I cannot see whether earlier sections define their terms. Three of my rewordings are interpretations that you should confirm; they are listed at the end.

## Violations

| Passage | Rule | Original phrase | Fix |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 3 | "The K rows of a run … masked when the run does not fill the block." | Split into four sentences. |
| 1 | 3 | "A run of one token, which is what every decode step produces, keeps the scatter." | Two sentences without the nested clause. |
| 1 | 1 | "claim the blocks from one counter" | "takes its next block from one shared counter" |
| 1 | 2 | "The generated plugin decides the helper count per pass; it is not a fixed number (7 helpers at tp2 …)." | Two sentences: the rule, then the measured example. |
| 1 | 3 | "Single-worker callers (…) and passes of at most 16 tokens store on the calling thread." | Verb first, then the two cases. |
| 2 | 1 | "Where write loses instead" | "Where write does worse than read" |
| 2 | 3 | "In the rows where write keeps less than read (…), the writers share a path that … (section 8)." | Split into five sentences. |
| 2 | 1 | "DRAM write ceiling" | "maximum DRAM write rate" |
| 3 | 4 | "the rows can show whether …, whether … and whether …, and whether …" | Bulleted list of three items. |
| 3 | 3 | "They cannot by themselves separate … and the external-fetch count … on the target." | Two explanations as a list; the counter gap as its own sentence. |
| 3 | 1 | "your picture" (2 uses) | "your hypothesis" |
| 3 | 1 | "aim at the L3" | "target the L3" |
| 3 | 1 | "data waiting in the L3 ahead of the core" | "the data is already in the L3 before the core requests it" |
| 3 | 1 | "a counter's source and population" | "where its values come from, and which events it counts" |
| 3 | 1 | "the one intervention on the table that acts on your picture directly" | "Of the interventions under consideration, only … directly changes the mechanism in your hypothesis" |

## Corrected text

Passage 1:
```
- Block save. A run is up to 16 consecutive tokens that fall in one 16-token block. The block save transposes the K rows of the run in registers. It then writes them as whole 64-byte cache lines, one store per line. When the run does not fill the block, each store uses a mask, so it writes only the part of the line that belongs to the run. Every decode step produces a run of one token. A run of one token still uses the scatter store.
- Sharing. The main thread and the idle main helper threads share the blocks. Each thread takes its next block from one shared counter. The helper count is not fixed: the generated plugin chooses it for each pass. In the traced runs at tp2, there were 7 helpers. In two cases the calling thread does all the stores: single-worker callers (the handwritten plugins and the unit tests), and passes of at most 16 tokens.
```

Passage 2:
```
Where write does worse than read. Write keeps less than read in two kinds of rows: two writers in one DSU at 160 KiB, and eight writers at any size. In those rows, the writers share one path. The limit on that path is either the mesh port of one DSU or the maximum DRAM write rate (section 8). Each write stream runs at 32 GB/s, and each read stream runs at only 9 to 12 GB/s. The write streams therefore saturate the shared path sooner than the read streams do.
```

Passage 3:
```
Codex gave this closing assessment, and the plan now states it.

The rows can show three things:

- whether the gain needs the prefetchers;
- whether the prefetchers target the L3, and whether demand reads find their cache lines there;
- whether more requests wait at the home nodes.

The rows alone cannot separate two explanations:

- Your hypothesis: the data is already in the L3 before the core requests it.
- The alternative: the DSU handles the same prefetch requests faster.

The external-fetch count with the L3 on stays "Insufficient data" until two facts about a counter are established on the target machine: where its values come from, and which events it counts.

Of the interventions under consideration, only the bit-6 boot directly changes the mechanism in your hypothesis.
```

## Not fixed

- **Rule 8 terms.** These need a definition unless an earlier section of the source document gives one:
  - Passage 1: K rows, tp2, pass, generated plugin, main helper threads.
  - Passage 2: DSU, mesh port.
  - Passage 3: Codex, home nodes, bit-6 boot, external-fetch count, "the gain".
- **Passage 2, "keeps less than read".** The sentence does not name the quantity that write keeps. Insufficient data: the column heading of the table these rows come from would resolve it.
- **Passage 2, "160 KiB".** The sentence does not say what this size measures. Insufficient data: the same table would resolve it.

## My readings to confirm

- **"ahead of the core"**: I read this as time (before the core requests the data), not as position.
- **"source and population"**: I read this as where the counter's values come from, and which set of events it counts.
- **"acts on your picture directly"**: I read this as "changes the mechanism that your hypothesis describes", not only "measures it".
